title: A Dead Star’s Shroud
caption: The planetary nebula EGB 6, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The planetary nebula EGB 6 resembles a vast bubble in space. It was captured with the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope, which stands at Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO).

Planetary nebulae, despite the name, are unrelated to planets. They arise in the final millennia of intermediate-mass stars, those with between one and eight times the Sun's mass. Near the end of its life such a star becomes a red giant, as fusion temporarily reignites in its core. Layers of gas shed during that phase soak up huge amounts of energy and glow as a planetary nebula.

Those 'dying millennia' last only about 20,000 years. That is a mere blink compared with the lives of these stars, which shine steadily for between 30 million and 10 billion years, with heavier stars at the shorter end.

understand.summary: Taken with the Mosaic I camera on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope through [O III] and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
